summary: Defines a static dictionary of common SIP and SDP text for use with Signaling Compression. Because both protocols are text-based and verbose, seeding the compressor with typical strings helps shrink messages, which matters on slow links such as mobile networks.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives SigComp a shared list of common SIP and SDP text. A compressor can use that list immediately, so it does not have to wait for earlier messages to build useful compression state.

questions: what is the sip sdp static dictionary
how do you compress sip messages
why compress sip over slow links
subtitle: A permanent dictionary lets SigComp compress common SIP and SDP text from the first message.

tldr.problem: SIP and SDP carry text, and their first compressed message has no earlier message state to reuse. That delay matters on narrow links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a fixed collection of common SIP and SDP strings as a SigComp state. Compressors can refer to it from the first message.
tldr.outcome: The dictionary is a shared, unchanging reference for compression. RFC 3485 is updated by RFC 4896.

facts.label: Priority values
facts.value: 1 to 5; lower number means more likely

today: RFC 3485 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2003, and is updated by RFC 4896. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why SIP and SDP Need Compression
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) sets up communication sessions, and the Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. Both are text-based. The RFC says that sending them over narrow links can substantially increase session setup time.

Signaling Compression (SigComp) compresses and decompresses text protocols. Its compression improves after messages have been exchanged, because later messages can use stored state. RFC 3485 supplies a shared state so the first message can also use common SIP and SDP text.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP and SDP messages can take longer to send over narrow links. A shared text dictionary helps the first message use compression too.

sections.title: How the Dictionary Is Organized
sections.content:
The dictionary contains strings that commonly appear in SIP and SDP messages. It is not a complete list of every reserved word. Every SigComp implementation for SIP and SDP MUST have this same dictionary, and the dictionary is defined once rather than changing as those protocols change.

Strings are case-sensitive and carry priorities from 1 to 5. Priority 1 means the authors consider a string more likely to occur than one with a higher number. Lower-numbered priorities are placed later in the dictionary, where some compression algorithms can use them more efficiently. Some less frequent strings are split so shared parts can be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: The dictionary contains selected common strings, not every possible protocol word. It never changes, and its priority values place likely strings where compression algorithms can use them.

sections.title: The Binary Dictionary State
sections.content:
The normative dictionary is a SigComp state value made from two joined parts. The string subset contains the dictionary text, with shared substrings able to occupy the same space. The table subset stores a length and offset for each string; each length uses one byte and each offset uses two bytes with 1024 added.

The full state has a length of 0x12E4 and a minimum access length of 6. The string subset is 0x0D8C bytes and the table subset is 0x0558 bytes. Compression algorithms can use the strings; methods related to LZ78 can also use the table to create initial tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: The state stores the text strings and a separate index of their lengths and locations. A compressor can use the strings, and some methods can also use the index.

sections.title: Accessing the State in SigComp
sections.content:
A SigComp program accesses the dictionary with the STATE-ACCESS instruction. It supplies the first six bytes of the state identifier as a partial identifier, then specifies where the requested part should be copied in UDVM memory.

An implementation can load only strings up to a chosen priority to save memory. The RFC provides offsets and lengths for each supported priority range. Lower-numbered priorities are stored at the end of the string subset, so the selected ranges can be accessed as portions of that subset.
sections.plainLanguage: SigComp asks for the dictionary by its identifier and copies the needed part into memory. An implementation with less memory can load only the priority range it needs.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for SigComp in RFC 3320 also apply to this dictionary. RFC 3485 says it introduces no known additional security risk. Its IANA considerations state that there are no actions.

The dictionary is a fixed set of protocol text used to aid compression. It does not define a new signaling exchange or change the security mechanisms described by SigComp.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says SigComp's existing security guidance still applies and this dictionary adds no known security risk. It requests no IANA assignment.
